# ADR-0019: A partitioning may sit in a rotated frame, recorded with the source

> **Status:** proposed | **Date:** 2026-08-01

**References:** [RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec), [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo), [RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit), [RFC-0003:C-PARTITIONING](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-partitioning), [ADR-0018](../adr/ADR-0018.md)

## Context

A survey strip running diagonally across the axes its source is expressed in fills an axis-aligned tiling with
mostly-empty partitions. That is not merely wasteful storage: halo cost scales with boundary area, and an
ill-fitting tiling is exactly what maximises boundary area per point. Aligning a partitioning to the data
addresses tile count, halo volume and occupancy together.

Nothing in the corpus required partitions to be axis-aligned. [RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec) 4 obliges bounds to be
declared and says nothing about their orientation, and [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 1 states what an alteration to
positions must preserve rather than which alterations are permitted. So the question was never whether
orientation is forbidden, but whether the corpus should say anything at all.

The literature says yes and does it per node. A directional binary space partitioning computes each node's
orientation by principal component analysis and applies a Karhunen–Loève transform to the coordinates inside
that node, on the stated ground that regular equal division "is not consistent with the irregular and
non-uniform distribution of most point clouds" and that axis-aligned division leaves empty space in its
bounding boxes. It reports tighter volumes, faster rendering and lower memory.

Production is unanimous the other way, and that work's own survey says so: existing methods are all axis-aligned
with regular tree structure. Cloud-optimised point clouds, Entwine point tiles, Potree, LAStools and PDAL all
partition on an axis-aligned lattice, and a voxelised root subdividing per level *is* such a lattice.

The reason is node identity. A node key is a level plus integer coordinates on a global lattice, which is what
makes range-readable access work — and in Strider it is what [RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit) 3 derives its fixed
reduction order from. Per-node orientation destroys that lattice: a key is no longer computable from a
position, and two nodes' frames are not commensurable. That last part is the specific obstacle here, because a
halo crosses partition boundaries by construction. Under per-partition frames, halo points arrive in a
different frame from the core points they serve, and the grid-alignment reasoning in [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 3 has
no common grid to reason about.

Three obligations already in the corpus constrain any answer, and an earlier draft of this decision collided
with all three: coordinates may be transformed only through an explicit operator; a library crate must treat a
coordinate reference system as opaque, so it may not compose one; and a committed run's partitioning may draw
on nothing but the source's index and what the operators declared.

## Decision

A partitioning may be established over coordinates in a frame reached from the source's by a rigid motion,
provided the frame is settled before the source is used and travels with it. [RFC-0003:C-PARTITIONING](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-partitioning) 4
carries the obligation and the three conditions that reconcile it with the rest of the corpus, together with
why the recording is the only thing made mandatory. This decision covers what that clause defers: which class
of motion, and how many frames.

**The class is the rigid motions, and the reason is a coincidence worth naming.** Three quantities have to
survive for a partitioning to still describe its data. Halo widths are distances, so the motion must preserve
distance. Membership is a containment test, so the motion must preserve which side of a surface a point falls.
Reduction order comes from spatial index keys rather than from coordinates, so the motion must leave keys
alone. A rigid motion is precisely the class that satisfies the first two, and the third it satisfies by not
being about coordinates at all. Nothing weaker will do: a scaling breaks the first, and a projection breaks it
non-uniformly, which is worse because a single declared width then bounds different neighbourhoods in different
parts of an extent.

Translation deserves separate mention because it is nearly free. Coordinates are stored as integers scaled
about an offset, so a shift is a change to that offset and touches no integer. It is also the one motion that
costs no precision, where reprojection forces requantisation and a coarser quantum to declare.

**One frame, as advice rather than as a rule.** The alternative with published results behind it orients every
node separately, and reports tighter volumes for doing so. Its cost falls on two things this project relies on.
Node keys are computed from position on a shared lattice, and per-node frames leave no shared lattice to compute
them from. More narrowly but more decisively: a halo is defined by crossing a partition boundary, so a
per-partition frame guarantees that the points a halo supplies were expressed in a different frame from the
points they serve — and the reasoning about aligning a summary grid to partition boundaries has no single grid
left to align.

Neither of those is a proof that per-node frames cannot be made to work, and the tighter volumes are real. That
asymmetry is why the clause advises one frame instead of requiring it: the reasons are strong enough to steer an
implementation and not strong enough to foreclose one that has measured otherwise.

## Consequences

### Positive

The occupancy benefit becomes reachable without adding orientation to the bounding-volume model: bounds stay
axis-aligned *in the frame the source declares*, so node keys, the reduction order derived from them, halo
widths and grid-alignment reasoning are all untouched. The mechanism is one Strider already permits — the
isometry case of [ADR-0018](../adr/ADR-0018.md)'s displacement duty — applied once where the source is written rather than
mid-pipeline.

### Negative

A source may now be expressed in a frame that is not the one its data was surveyed in, and every consumer
depends on the recording to place it. That is one more thing a badly written source can omit, and its failure
mode is silent misplacement rather than an error.

The permission also has a reach limit that is not obvious from its text. A rotated frame and a summary grid
defined in the source's original frame cannot generally have coinciding boundaries, so the reduced summary halo
[RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 3 permits on boundary coincidence becomes unavailable in such a frame. That is a cost paid
in halo volume, partly offsetting the saving this decision exists to obtain, and it is unmeasured.

### Neutral

Whether a partition's bounds may be **oriented** rather than axis-aligned is still not decided, and this
decision deliberately does not decide it. It offers a way to get most of the benefit while keeping bounds
axis-aligned, which makes oriented volumes less pressing rather than unnecessary. If registration or levelling
later wants to keep its partitioning across a general rotation, that is the moment to decide whether
[RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec) 4's bounds admit an orientation — a question that ripples into extent restriction and into
how partitions are keyed.

Two quantities behind this are unmeasured and should not be mistaken for evidence: the actual occupancy gain on
a diagonal strip, and whether a single global rotation captures most of what per-node analysis would.

## Alternatives Considered

### Permit a partitioning over coordinates in a frame related to the source's by an isometry, fixed before any run and recorded with the source, advising one frame per partitioning (accepted)

- **Pros:** Bounds stay axis-aligned in the declared frame, so node keys and the reduction order derived from them are untouched, Halo widths stay commensurable across partitions, which per-partition frames would break since a halo crosses boundaries, Uses a mechanism already permitted — the isometry case of the displacement duty — rather than a new one, A permission, so an implementation that does not want it opts out of nothing
- **Cons:** A source may be expressed in a frame its data was not surveyed in, and consumers depend on the recording to place it, Boundary coincidence with a summary grid in the original frame is generally unachievable, so the reduced summary halo becomes unavailable

### Say nothing: leave the corpus silent on frames, as it was (rejected)

- **Pros:** No new obligation, no new failure mode, nothing to record, Silence already permits it, since nothing required axis-aligned bounds
- **Cons:** Silence also permits doing it without recording the frame, whose failure is silent misplacement, Leaves an implementer to rediscover per-node orientation and break the lattice, which is the attractive wrong answer
- **Rejected because:** The permission is not what needed writing; the recording obligation is. Silence leaves the one part with a silent failure mode ungoverned, and leaves the lattice-breaking approach looking equally available.

### Orient each partition independently by principal component analysis, transforming coordinates within each node, as the directional BSP literature does (rejected)

- **Pros:** Reported tighter bounding volumes than a single rotation, with faster rendering at lower memory, Adapts to data whose distribution changes across the extent, which one global frame cannot
- **Cons:** Destroys the global lattice: a node key is no longer computable from a position, so the fixed reduction order loses its basis, A halo crosses partition boundaries by construction, so halo points would arrive in a different frame from the core points they serve, Grid-alignment reasoning for a summary halo has no common grid left to reason about
- **Rejected because:** The costs land squarely on machinery the corpus already depends on — node-key-derived reduction order, and commensurable halo widths across a boundary a halo must cross. These are reasons for one frame rather than proofs the approach cannot work, which is why the clause advises one frame instead of forbidding this.
